chunks: Achieving faster slew rates in CMOS. The question: How can you achieve faster slew rates?
Slew rate is how fast a signal's voltage can change. For a capacitive load it equals the current you can supply divided by the capacitance.
So to get faster edges, supply more current, reduce the capacitance, or make the voltage swing smaller.
Picture filling a balloon with a hose. A wider hose fills it faster, and a smaller balloon fills sooner. You get a fast fill by using a big hose on a small balloon.
But a big hose gushing suddenly makes a jolt, just as fast electrical edges cause spikes and ringing.
Same 50 picofarads load, three driver strengths. Rise time scales linearly with R on : wider drivers give proportionally faster edges.
Past a point, other limits (package inductance, previous stage) take over.
Slew rate: how fast the voltage changes, in V per second ( dV over dt ). Load capacitance: how much charge the load soaks up per volt, from traces, pins and inputs.
Measured in farads; 1 picofarads is a millionth of a millionth of a farad. Drive strength: how much current an output can supply, set by its W over L .
Fan-out: how many inputs the output drives, which adds load. Ground bounce: a voltage spike on ground caused by large fast current changes.
Say an output can deliver 10 milliamps into a 10 picofarads load.
The slew rate is I over C equals 10 milliamps over 10 picofarads equals 10 to the 9 volts/s, which is 1 volts per nanosecond. A 3. 3 volts swing then takes about 3. 3 nanoseconds.
Double the drive current to 20 milliamps and the edge becomes twice as fast. That is the whole idea.
"Slew rate is I over C , so to go faster I increase drive current, reduce capacitance, or reduce swing.

In CMOS that means wider output transistors for lower on-resistance, more gate overdrive or a higher supply, and a tapered chain of inverters, each about 3 to 4 times larger than the last, to drive big output devices.
I'd also cut the load capacitance by shortening traces and reducing fan-out.
The trade-off is peak current, ground bounce, ringing and EMI, so I'd choose the slowest edge that meets timing."
